sentences.en: Good morning, everyone.
sentences.zh: 大家早上好。

sentences.en: My name is David and I am good at arguing.
sentences.zh: 我叫戴维，我很擅长辩论。

sentences.en: So welcome to our introductory lecture on argumentation.
sentences.zh: 欢迎来到我们的论证学入门讲座。

sentences.en: Why do we want to argue?
sentences.zh: 我们为什么想要争辩呢？

sentences.en: Why do we try to convince other people to believe things that they don’t want to believe?
sentences.zh: 我们为什么要设法说服别人相信他们原本不愿相信的事情？

sentences.en: And is that even a nice thing to do?
sentences.zh: 而且，这样做真的好吗？

sentences.en: Is that a nice way to treat other human being, try and make them think something they don’t want to think?
sentences.zh: 设法让别人去想他们原本不愿想的事情，这样对待他人算友善吗？

sentences.en: Well, my answer is going to make reference to three models for arguments.
sentences.zh: 我的回答会涉及三种论证模式。

sentences.en: The first model—let’s call this the dialectical model—is that we think of arguments as war.
sentences.zh: 第一种模式，我们姑且称之为辩证模式，就是把论证看成战争。

sentences.en: And you know what that’s like.
sentences.zh: 你们知道那是什么样的。

sentences.en: There is a lot of screaming and shouting and winning and losing.
sentences.zh: 其中充斥着尖叫、大喊，以及输赢之争。

sentences.en: And that’s not really a very helpful model for arguing, but it’s a pretty common and fixed one.
sentences.zh: 这其实不是一种很有帮助的论证模式，但它确实相当常见，而且根深蒂固。

sentences.en: I guess you must have seen that type of arguing many times—in the street, on the bus or in the subway.
sentences.zh: 我想，你们一定在街上、公交车上或地铁里，见过很多次这样的争吵。

sentences.en: Let’s move on to the second model.
sentences.zh: 我们接着来看第二种模式。

sentences.en: The second model for arguing regards arguments as proofs.
sentences.zh: 第二种论证模式把论证看成证明。

sentences.en: Think of a mathematician’s argument.
sentences.zh: 想一想数学家的论证。

sentences.en: Here’s my argument.
sentences.zh: 这是我的论证。

sentences.en: Does it work?
sentences.zh: 它成立吗？

sentences.en: Is it any good?
sentences.zh: 它是否合理？

sentences.en: Are the premises warranted?
sentences.zh: 这些前提有充分根据吗？

sentences.en: Are the inferences valid?
sentences.zh: 这些推理有效吗？

sentences.en: Does the conclusion follow the premises?
sentences.zh: 结论能从前提中推导出来吗？

sentences.en: No opposition, no adversariality—not necessarily any arguing in the adversarial sense.
sentences.zh: 这里没有对立，也没有敌对，并不一定涉及敌对意义上的争辩。

sentences.en: And there’s a third model to keep in mind that I think is going to be very helpful, and that is arguments as performances, arguments as being in front of an audience.
sentences.zh: 还有第三种值得记住的模式，我认为它会很有用：把论证看成表演，也就是在听众面前展开论证。

sentences.en: We can think of a politician trying to present a position, trying to convince the audience of something.
sentences.zh: 可以想象一位政治人物试图阐明某种立场，并说服听众接受它。

sentences.en: But there’s another twist on this model that I really think is important; namely, that when we argue before an audience, sometimes the audience has a more participatory role in the argument; that is, you present your arguments in front of an audience who are like juries that make a judgment and decide the case.
sentences.zh: 不过，我认为这种模式还有一个重要的变体：在听众面前论证时，听众有时会更多地参与进来；也就是说，听众就像陪审团，会作出判断并裁决结果。

sentences.en: Let’s call this model the rhetorical model, where you have to tailor your argument to the audience at hand.
sentences.zh: 我们把这种模式称为修辞模式，在这种模式中，你必须根据眼前的听众调整论证。

sentences.en: Of those three, the argument as war is the dominant one.
sentences.zh: 在这三种模式中，把论证视为战争的模式占据主导地位。

sentences.en: It dominates how we talk about arguments, it dominates how we think about arguments, and because of that, it shapes how we argue, our actual conduct in arguments.
sentences.zh: 它支配着我们谈论论证和思考论证的方式，因此也塑造了我们如何论证，以及我们在论证中的实际行为。

sentences.en: We want strong arguments, arguments that have a lot of punch, arguments that are right on target.
sentences.zh: 我们想要强有力、冲击力十足、一针见血的论点。

sentences.en: We want to have our defenses up and our strategies all in order.
sentences.zh: 我们希望做好防守，安排好所有策略。

sentences.en: We want killer arguments.
sentences.zh: 我们想要能一击制胜的论点。

w.m: adj.极有杀伤力的；极有说服力的

sentences.en: That’s the kind of argument we want.
sentences.zh: 这就是我们想要的那种论证。

sentences.en: It is the dominant way of thinking about arguments.
sentences.zh: 这是思考论证时占主导地位的方式。

sentences.en: When I’m talking about arguments, that’s probably what you thought of, the adversarial model.
sentences.zh: 我一谈到论证，你们想到的大概就是这种对抗模式。

sentences.en: But the war metaphor, the war paradigm or model for thinking about arguments, has, I think, negative effects on how we argue.
sentences.zh: 但我认为，战争这个隐喻，也就是用来思考论证的战争范式或模式，会对我们的论证方式产生负面影响。

sentences.en: First, it elevates tactics over substance.
sentences.zh: 首先，它把策略置于实质内容之上。

sentences.en: You can take a class in logic argumentation.
sentences.zh: 你可以去上一门逻辑论证课程。

sentences.en: You learn all about the strategies that people use to try and win arguments and that makes arguing adversarial; it’s polarizing.
sentences.zh: 你会学到人们试图赢得论战时使用的各种策略，而这让论证变得具有对抗性，使人们走向两极。

sentences.en: And the only foreseeable outcomes are triumph—glorious triumph—or disgraceful defeat.
sentences.zh: 唯一可以预见的结果，就是胜利，辉煌的胜利，或是耻辱的失败。

sentences.en: I think those are very destructive effects, and worst of all, it seems to prevent things like negotiation and collaboration.
sentences.zh: 我认为这些影响极具破坏性；更糟的是，这种模式似乎会阻碍协商与合作之类的事情。

sentences.en: Um, I think the argument-as-war metaphor inhibits those other kinds of resolutions to argumentation.
sentences.zh: 我认为，把论证视为战争的隐喻，会抑制其他解决争论的方式。

sentences.en: And finally—this is really the worst thing—arguments don’t seem to get us anywhere; they’re dead ends.
sentences.zh: 最后，也是最糟的一点，争论似乎让我们毫无进展，走进了死胡同。

w.m: phr.死胡同；没有出路的局面

sentences.en: We don’t get anywhere.
sentences.zh: 我们没有取得任何进展。

sentences.en: Oh, and one more thing.
sentences.zh: 哦，还有一件事。

sentences.en: That is, if argument is war, then there’s also an implicit aspect of meaning—learning with losing.
sentences.zh: 也就是说，如果论证就是战争，那么其中还暗含着另一层意义：在失败中学习。

sentences.en: And let me explain what I mean.
sentences.zh: 让我解释一下我的意思。

sentences.en: Suppose you and I have an argument.
sentences.zh: 假设你和我展开一场争论。

sentences.en: You believe a proposition and I don’t.
sentences.zh: 你相信某个命题，而我不相信。

sentences.en: And I say, “Well, why do you believe that?”
sentences.zh: 我问你：“你为什么相信它呢？”

sentences.en: And you give me your reasons.
sentences.zh: 于是你给出了你的理由。

sentences.en: And I object and say, “Well, what about...?”
sentences.zh: 我表示反对，并问：“那么……又怎么解释呢？”

sentences.en: And you answer my objection.
sentences.zh: 你回应了我的异议。

sentences.en: And I have a question: “Well, what do you mean? How does it apply over here?”
sentences.zh: 接着我又有问题：“你是什么意思？这又怎么适用于这里呢？”

sentences.en: And you answer my question.
sentences.zh: 你又回答了我的问题。

sentences.en: Now, suppose at the end of the day, I’ve objected, I’ve questioned, I’ve raised all sorts of questions from an opposite perspective and in every case you’ve responded to my satisfaction.
sentences.zh: 现在，假设到最后，我已经提出过异议、追问过问题、从相反的角度提出过种种疑问，而每次你都给出了让我满意的回应。

sentences.en: And so at the end of the day, I say, “You know what? I guess you’re right.”
sentences.zh: 最后我说：“你知道吗？我想你是对的。”

sentences.en: Maybe finally I lost my argument.
sentences.zh: 也许最终是我输掉了这场争论。

sentences.en: But isn’t it also a process of learning?
sentences.zh: 但这不也是一个学习的过程吗？

sentences.en: So you see arguments may also have positive effects.
sentences.zh: 所以你们看，论证也可能产生积极影响。

sentences.en: So, how can we find new ways to achieve those positive effects?
sentences.zh: 那么，我们怎样才能找到实现这些积极影响的新方式呢？

sentences.en: We need to think of new kinds of arguments.
sentences.zh: 我们需要思考新类型的论证。

sentences.en: Here I have some suggestions.
sentences.zh: 我有一些建议。

sentences.en: If we want to think of new kinds of arguments, what we need to do is think of new kinds of arguers—people who argue.
sentences.zh: 如果我们想思考新类型的论证，就需要思考新类型的论辩者，也就是参与论辩的人。

sentences.en: So try this: Think of all the roles that people play in arguments.
sentences.zh: 不妨试一试：想想人们在论证中扮演的所有角色。

sentences.en: There’s the proponent and the opponent in an adversarial, dialectical argument.
sentences.zh: 在对抗性的辩证论证中，有提出主张的人和反对主张的人。

sentences.en: There’s the audience in rhetorical arguments.
sentences.zh: 在修辞论证中，有听众。

sentences.en: There’s the reasoner in arguments as proofs.
sentences.zh: 在作为证明的论证中，有进行推理的人。

sentences.en: All these different roles.
sentences.zh: 这些都是不同的角色。

sentences.en: Now, can you imagine an argument in which you are the arguer, but you’re also in the audience, watching yourself argue?
sentences.zh: 现在，你能否想象这样一场论证：你既是论辩者，也是听众，在旁观看自己论辩？

sentences.en: Can you imagine yourself watching yourself argue?
sentences.zh: 你能想象自己旁观自己论辩的样子吗？

sentences.en: That means you need to be supported by yourself.
sentences.zh: 这意味着你需要给自己支持。

sentences.en: Even when you lose the argument, still, at the end of the argument, you could say, “Wow, that was a good argument!”
sentences.zh: 即使输掉论证，到最后你仍然可以说：“哇，这真是一场精彩的论证！”

sentences.en: Can you do that?
sentences.zh: 你能做到吗？

sentences.en: I think you can.
sentences.zh: 我想你可以。

sentences.en: In this way, you’ve been supported by yourself.
sentences.zh: 这样一来，你就给了自己支持。

sentences.en: Up till now, I have lost a lot of arguments.
sentences.zh: 到现在为止，我已经输掉过很多次争论。

sentences.en: It really takes practice to become a good arguer, in the sense of being able to benefit from losing, but fortunately, I’ve had many, many colleagues who have been willing to step up and provide that practice for me.
sentences.zh: 要成为一个好的论辩者，能够从失败中获益，确实需要练习；幸运的是，我有许多同事愿意挺身而出，让我有机会练习。

sentences.en: OK.
sentences.zh: 好的。

sentences.en: To sum up, in today’s lecture, I have introduced three models of arguments.
sentences.zh: 总结一下，在今天的讲座中，我介绍了三种论证模式。

sentences.en: The first model is called the dialectical model.
sentences.zh: 第一种叫作辩证模式。

sentences.en: The second one is the model of arguments as proofs.
sentences.zh: 第二种是把论证看成证明的模式。

sentences.en: And the last one is called the rhetorical model, the model of arguments as performances.
sentences.zh: 最后一种叫作修辞模式，也就是把论证看成表演的模式。

sentences.en: I have also emphasized that, though the adversarial type of arguments is quite common, we can still make arguments produce some positive effects.
sentences.zh: 我也强调了，虽然对抗式论证非常常见，但我们仍然可以让论证产生一些积极影响。

sentences.en: Next time I will continue our discussion on the process of arguing.
sentences.zh: 下次我会继续讨论论证的过程。
